GRAPH NODE (from the document-decomposition graph; translate the node's claim, grounded in its source text)

ESTABLISHES (the one claim this module must express):
The approach of bounding autonomy by scope mirrors the principle of least privilege and capability-based security common in software security, and scope should not be so narrow as to require multiple confirmations by the user for trivial actions, which could habituate the user to automatically confirming all requests.

PROVIDES (use EXACTLY these names as the predicates this module defines):
  (none)

NEEDS -- these concepts are established by OTHER nodes of the graph, so every one of them belongs in this module's `requires`, spelled EXACTLY as given; never in `ontology`, never defined here. `inputs` is only for plain facts about the situation being judged (messages, roles, case data) that YOU identify -- a name can never appear in both requires and inputs:
  - scope_of_autonomy: The agreed-upon boundary of the assistant's autonomy, defining which sub-goals it may pursue, acceptable side effects, and when it must pause for clarification or approval.
  - root_authority: Rules in the #scope_of_autonomy section carry root authority.

CITATION: every ontology/asserts entry that cites a source must cite EXACTLY 'l461_608_n005' -- the id of this node. Never cite line numbers, line ranges, or any other id.

SOURCE TEXT (verbatim from the document; the L-numbers locate text, they are not citable ids):
L0480-L0481:
    This approach mirrors the [principle of least privilege](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principle_of_least_privilege) and [capability-based security](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capability-based_security) common in software security. Striking the right balance is important,
    as scope should also not be so narrow as to require multiple confirmations by the user for trivial actions, which could habituate the user to automatically confirming all requests.
